title: The test pyramid and coverage
summary: Which tests to run where, and what a coverage number does and does not tell you.

steps.title: The pyramid
body: ```text
/\         end-to-end (UI, full system)   few · slow · brittle · high confidence per test
/----\       integration (API + real DB)     some
/--------\     unit (one class, no I/O)       many · milliseconds · precise failures
Unit tests are cheap, fast and tell you exactly what broke, so you want **lots** of them. End-to-end tests prove the system works
as a whole but are slow and fail for reasons unrelated to your change (timeouts, test data), so you want **few**.
The anti-pattern is the **ice-cream cone**: mostly manual and end-to-end tests, few unit tests. Pipelines get slow and red for no reason.

steps.prompt: Which layer does each test belong to?
items: `POST /orders` against the API with a real PostgreSQL container
The repository's SQL query returns orders by customer
A browser logs in, adds to cart and checks out
The deployed staging site's sign-up email arrives

steps.title: Where each layer runs
body: Not every test runs on every event. A common split:
| Event | Runs | Budget |
| every push / PR | unit + integration | < 10 min |
| merge to main | + build image, deploy to staging, smoke tests | < 30 min |
| nightly | full end-to-end and load tests | hours |
A **smoke test** is a handful of checks right after a deploy ("does `/health` answer 200? can I log in?") that catches a broken release fast.

steps.prompt: A PR pipeline takes 55 minutes because it runs 400 browser tests. Developers have started merging without waiting. What is the best first step?
options: Move most behaviour checks down to unit/integration tests and run the browser suite nightly or after merge
Buy faster runners and keep everything
Run the browser tests only on Fridays
steps.explain: Feedback that is too slow is ignored. Push checks down the pyramid; keep a small end-to-end set where it adds real confidence.

steps.title: Coverage
body: **Line coverage** = lines executed by tests ÷ executable lines. In .NET: `dotnet test --collect:"XPlat Code Coverage"` writes a Cobertura XML report.
```text
file            covered  total   %
Pricing.cs         45      50   90.0
Orders.cs          30      60   50.0
total              75     110   68.2     (not the average 70.0!)
Coverage tells you what is **definitely untested**. High coverage does not prove the tests check anything: a test with no assertions still
covers every line it runs. Use it as a floor and a trend, not a target to game.

steps.prompt: Two files: `A.cs` covers 10 of 10 lines, `B.cs` covers 0 of 90 lines. What total line coverage does the report show (one decimal)?
steps.explain: Totals are computed from summed lines: 10 ÷ 100. Averaging per-file percentages would wrongly give 50%.

steps.prompt: Match each check to its purpose.
pairs: is the freshly deployed app alive at all?
does the API still match what its consumers expect?
does it hold up at peak traffic?
does this one piece of logic behave?

steps.title: Shape of the suite
prompt: Write `string SuiteShape(int unit, int integration, int e2e)`:
starter: string SuiteShape(int unit, int integration, int e2e)
solution: string SuiteShape(int unit, int integration, int e2e)
if (e2e > integration && integration > unit) return "ice-cream cone";
hints: C# has no chained `a > b > c`; write two comparisons joined by `&&`.
template: Dojo.Eq("ties are not a pyramid", "other", SuiteShape(100, 100, 5));

steps.title: Total coverage
prompt: Write `double TotalCoverage(List<(string File, int Covered, int Total)> files)` returning the total line coverage as a percentage,
rounded to one decimal place with `Math.Round(x, 1)`. With no executable lines at all, return `0`.
starter: double TotalCoverage(List<(string File, int Covered, int Total)> files)
solution: double TotalCoverage(List<(string File, int Covered, int Total)> files)
hints: Sum covered lines and total lines separately, then divide.
Use `100.0` so the division is not integer division.
